newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Sugar - China 1997 sugar imports seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China 1997 sugar imports seen unlikely.

text.p: China is unlikely to import sugar this year despite strong seasonal demand during the summer and ahead of the mid-autumn festival, as domestic stocks are expected to be sufficient to meet the market's needs, traders said on Friday.
Reflecting the rise in demand, prices in major growing areas in China have risen from around 4,200 yuan ($506) per tonne last week to up to 4,600 yuan, traders in Hong Kong said on Wednesday.

Consumption of sugar in the hot summer months rises due to greater demand for ice-cream and soft drinks, as well as preparations for the mid-autumn festival, celebrated with sticky, sweet moon cakes. The festival falls on September 16 this year.

"We have confirmed that sugar prices in China are rising rapidly at the moment, but this does not necessarily mean they (China) will start buying in the world market," a senior sugar trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Another Japanese sugar trader added, "China may consider buying sugar when prices rise above the 5,000 yuan level, but higher-than-normal sugar stock levels are still an obstacle."
Looking ahead to next year, however, he agreed with a recent report predicting that China would return to the world market in 1998.
Sugar trade house Czarnikow Sugar said on Thursday that China is likely to import sugar in 1998 as a result of an expected increase in consumption.

Thai raw sugar premiums for the January-March 1998 period were 1.05/1.20 U.S. cents per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange futures, on an FOB basis, and 1.00/1.10 cents for the March-May 1998 period, Japanese traders said.
Czarnikow Sugar estimated Thailand's sugar production in 1997/98 would fall by 725,000 tonnes to 5.35 million tonnes, based on cane production of 49 million tonnes.

"One of our staff who recently visited sugar growing areas in Thailand reported crop damage there due to drought. Thai premiums are expected to remain stable for a while," a third sugar trader at a trade house said.

Yen-based raw sugar futures on the Tokyo Grain Exchange rose sharply during the morning session on Friday, reflecting the yen's steep fall against dollar and modest gains in New York sugar futures overnight, local traders said.
Benchmark January 1999 rose by its daily 800 yen limit to 30,930 yen per tonne by late morning.

"The market rose sharply on light buying from individual investors, but compared with volatile corn and precious metal futures, open interest in raw sugar is still low," an analyst with a commodity brokerage house said.
